sentences.text: Visibility assessments are estimates of the conditions expected along a route and at a work site, rather than guarantees of clear sightlines.
Reported visibility can vary across the wind farm as fog banks, rain, spray, and low cloud move through the area.
Differences between observation times and locations can leave uncertainty even when individual reports are valid.
The Weather Service forecast provides context for expected changes, but local conditions may develop sooner or differently than forecast.
The Metocean Buoy provides a local reference that can help identify differences between forecast conditions and conditions at sea.
A discrepancy between sources prompts review of the observation age, location, and surrounding weather conditions.
The operational assessment records both the estimated visibility and the confidence that the estimate represents conditions at the intended work location.
Low confidence is treated as an operational constraint even when the reported visibility appears adequate.
The Duty Planner uses the Visibility Confidence Note when considering task readiness and the conditions that would require a decision to pause or defer work.
The Maintenance Planning Engine can help identify tasks that may be rescheduled when visibility is uncertain.
Task selection favors work that can be performed safely under the assessed conditions without relying on precise visual identification or close-range observation.
Work requiring visual alignment, external inspection, or unobstructed observation is given a more conservative assessment.
Use of the Blade Inspection Drone is deferred when uncertain visibility could prevent reliable control or interpretation of inspection imagery.
The go or no-go decision considers the task method, crew competence, vessel capability, and the confidence in the visibility assessment.
A favorable point estimate alone is not sufficient to authorize a task when the range of plausible conditions includes unsafe visibility.
The Marine Coordinator reviews how uncertainty affects the planned transit, transfer location, and available alternatives.
The Vessel Master retains authority to proceed, slow, alter course, or hold position based on actual conditions and vessel limits.
A Crew Transfer Vessel may be directed to remain clear of a transfer location until the crew and vessel can maintain adequate visual awareness.
A Daughter Craft operation requires particular caution where reduced visibility could compromise separation from other vessels or structures.
A Service Operations Vessel may maintain a safe stand-off while the visibility assessment is clarified.
Planned vessel movements account for reduced speed, increased separation, and the possibility of returning to a safe holding area.
When uncertainty increases during transit, the Marine Coordinator and Vessel Master reassess the route and the suitability of continuing toward the work site.
The Shore Control Room maintains awareness of the decision and the operational restrictions associated with the assessment.
A no-go decision is appropriate when uncertainty prevents the team from demonstrating that the transfer or task can be completed within safe limits.
Conditions are reassessed before work resumes, and authorization is based on current evidence rather than the earlier estimate.
